source_citation: DWP SSI JSA Statistics March 2016
notes: POPULATION BASE. All 2070 employed by SSI made redundant on 2 Oct 2015. List from Insolvency Service — high accuracy. All DWP figures rounded to nearest 10. Supply chain excluded due to incomplete records. Use 2070 as the correct denominator for all Redcar rates.
comparability_notes: Other sources cite 2200 or 2150 — these include supply chain estimates or all-benefit claimants. Do not mix denominators across rows.

source_citation: DWP SSI JSA Statistics March 2016
notes: 540 of 2070 (25%) still claiming JSA at end of Feb 2016. JSA requires active job search — captures workers not yet employed and not on other benefits. 65% (1350) claimed JSA at least once; of those 40% still on it at 5 months. Remaining 60% (810) ended JSA claim but DWP warns this does NOT mean re-employed — could be ESA / Universal Credit / Income Support / retirement / left UK.
comparability_notes: JSA-only measure. Workers who moved to ESA or UC appear as exited JSA but are not re-employed. Cannot compare directly to German or US studies using different benefit systems.

source_citation: DWP SSI JSA Statistics March 2016
notes: 720 workers (35%) made no JSA claim at all. DWP lists possible reasons: on other benefits (ESA/UC/Income Support); dependent on partner claim; chose to retire; temporarily re-employed by official receiver; left UK. Cannot be read as immediately re-employed. Task Force figure of 500+ claimed NO benefit at all — gap of ~220 likely on ESA or UC.
comparability_notes: Not claiming JSA is not the same as employed. Critical distinction when comparing to Hartz or China shock literature which use different administrative definitions.

source_citation: SSI Task Force One Year On Report Sept 2016
notes: 1990 of 2150 (93%) ended ALL benefit claims by 12 months. Task Force base of 2150 is larger than DWP 2070 because it covers ALL benefits not just JSA. ~160 workers (7%) still on benefits at 12 months — hard-to-place group likely older or health-affected. The 93% exit rate CANNOT be split into the 4 model buckets — retrain / similar / underemployed / exit are all lumped under exited benefits. This is the key data gap for Redcar.
comparability_notes: Most-cited Redcar statistic but least useful for calibration — conflates all positive outcomes. Without DWP microdata (restricted access) there is no clean split into the 4 outcome buckets from public sources.

source_citation: SSI Task Force One Year On Report Sept 2016
notes: 500+ workers (24% of 2070) made no benefit claim of any kind — likely split between early retirees (EXIT) and immediately re-employed workers. Cannot distinguish without further data. Compare to DWP figure of 720 who did not claim JSA — gap of ~220 likely on ESA or UC but not JSA.
comparability_notes: Early retirement and immediate re-employment look identical in this data. Steel sector has strong pensions so early retirement may be more common than in other sectors.

source_citation: SSI Task Force One Year On + Gov.uk 6-month press release
notes: NO CLEAN RETRAIN RATE AVAILABLE. 15510 training courses approved at 12 months; 4300 delivered by 6 months; 12000 applications across all schemes. These are course counts not worker counts — one worker may have taken multiple courses. 2988 workers received job advice (near-universal takeup given base of 2070). 50 former apprentices placed in training or employment — denominator unknown.
comparability_notes: UK training course ranges from a 2-day refresher to a full vocational qualification. German Umschulung in Hartz literature = full requalification of 1-2 years. Not directly comparable without knowing course type and duration.

source_citation: SSI Task Force One Year On Report Sept 2016
notes: SELF-EMPLOYMENT — not in model outcome set. 172 new businesses launched (8% of 2070); 418 received startup advice (20%). 821 new jobs created via SSI Fund; 410 safeguarded. Job creation counts are policy outputs not worker outcomes. Union reps confirmed workers in new jobs face lower pay — consistent with underemployment.
comparability_notes: Self-employment may be elevated in geographically isolated communities where re-employment options are scarce. Flag when comparing to Port Talbot or China shock data.

source_citation: Teesside Live — SSI 10 Years On Sept 2025
notes: 2-year figures: 315 new businesses (vs 172 at 12 months). £9m invested in 23000 training courses within 2 years — still course counts not worker counts so retrain rate still cannot be derived. Government funding cited as £53m here vs £46m (Task Force) / £50m (Teesside Live) / £80m (gov.uk). Discrepancy likely reflects tranched announcements. Use £46m as baseline.
comparability_notes: Funding figure inconsistency (£46m / £50m / £53m / £80m) is a genuine data quality issue — document and flag. Take Task Force own reported £46m as most credible.

source_citation: North East Times Magazine — Routes to Work scheme
notes: Routes to Work pilot (£7.5m): engaged 2800+ people across broader Tees Valley; 488 helped back into employment (17% of those engaged). Covers all Tees Valley long-term unemployed — NOT exclusively SSI workers. Two SSI worker case studies: (1) Ray Milner went Aberdeen bypass 2yr then Hinkley Point 2yr then Balfour Beatty then back to Redcar = SEEK_SIMILAR mobile trajectory. (2) Paul had unemployment with health challenges before Routes to Work = EXIT then re-entry.
comparability_notes: Routes to Work is a regional scheme not SSI-specific. Cannot use 17% as a Redcar-specific re-employment rate.

source_citation: Multiple press sources BBC / History Workshop / Local reporting
notes: 40% surge in area-wide JSA claimants immediately post-closure. Area-level — includes non-SSI workers but SSI was dominant cause. Consistent with DWP data showing claimant count rising 6% to 7% of working-age population. At least 160 former SSI staff remained unemployed at 12-month review per press summary of Task Force report.
comparability_notes: Area-level claimant surge is not directly comparable to individual worker outcomes. Use DWP individual-worker data (25% still on JSA at 5 months) as the primary measure.

source_citation: SSI Task Force / Gov.uk 6-month press release
notes: AGE BREAKDOWN — PARTIAL ONLY. 50%+ of workers seeking work were aged 45+. Employer subsidy age-tiered: £15k for hiring 45+ vs £11k for under 45 — government explicitly recognised older workers as harder to place implying higher exit risk. No outcome rates by age band available from any public source found.
comparability_notes: Age 45+ associated with higher exit probability in most displacement literature. Makes Redcar a harder-than-average episode. Check whether Hartz and China shock age distributions are comparable.

source_citation: Evidently Substack citing Tees Valley CA data
notes: UNDEREMPLOYMENT PROXY — area-level not individual. Area wages fell 0.5% real terms 2015-2017 vs +1.6% rest of North East = 2.1pp gap attributable to closure. Manual jobs fell 10% to 8% of local employment (Dec 2014 to Dec 2016); service sector rose 11% to 12% — occupational downshift consistent with steelworkers taking lower-paid service jobs. One documented worker applied to 50 jobs before finding one. Union confirmed lower pay in new roles.
comparability_notes: Wage data is area-level — cannot isolate SSI workers. However SSI was the dominant employer so effect is largely attributable to closure. Wage scarring is more comparable across episodes than benefit claim data.

source_citation: Evidently Substack citing Tees Valley CA data
notes: RECOVERY TIMELINE. Claimant count rose 6% to 7% post-closure (Sept-Nov 2015) and stayed elevated for ~2 years before returning to baseline Oct 2017. Best calibration point for how long displacement effects persist. Area-level measure covering Redcar and Cleveland not just SSI workers.
comparability_notes: 2-year recovery should be treated as best-case given large government support package. Unsupported closures likely take longer. Compare to Hartz (targeted unemployment duration) and China shock (much longer recovery in affected zones).

source_citation: Centre for Public Impact — Hartz Employment Reforms in Germany
subsidy_level: ALG II flat rate after 12 months ALG I
notes: CONTEXT ROW. Hartz I-IV implemented Jan 2003 to Jan 2005. Key changes: Hartz I-II eased temp work regulation and created mini-jobs up to €400/month. Hartz III restructured Federal Employment Agency. Hartz IV merged unemployment assistance and social assistance into ALG II flat-rate benefit. ALG I (insurance) duration cut from up to 32 months to max 12 months (18 months for 55+). After ALG I exhaustion workers move to means-tested ALG II ~€400/month. Tightened job search obligations — must accept any reasonable offer. Germany-wide national reform — NOT a single displacement episode. Population base is all German unemployed not a specific displaced cohort.
comparability_notes: CRITICAL: Hartz is a national policy reform affecting all unemployed Germans. Redcar and Port Talbot are single-site displacement episodes. Do not directly compare outcome rates. Use Hartz data as evidence for what happens when benefit/subsidy levels change (policy lever effects) not as a baseline displacement outcome rate.

source_citation: Centre for Public Impact + multiple IZA/IAB sources
notes: UNEMPLOYMENT RATE TRAJECTORY. Pre-reform 2002: ~13.4% including labour scheme participants. 2005 post-reform: ~11%. 2012: ~5.5%. End of 2014: ~5%. Overall reduction ~8-9pp over the decade. Portion attributable to Hartz reforms estimated at ~1.5pp (Odendahl CER 2017) — remainder due to broader economic recovery and wage moderation. ~2.5 million jobs credited to reforms though causality disputed. Long-term unemployment did NOT noticeably decrease per Gustav Horn — benefits of reform accrued mainly to those already with strong employment prospects.
comparability_notes: The 8-9pp unemployment decline conflates Hartz effects with broader economic recovery 2003-2008 and 2009 crisis response. The reform-attributable 1.5pp reduction (Odendahl) is the most credible isolated estimate. Do not use overall decline as a Hartz effect.

source_citation: Price 2020 IZA DP13300 + Kuegler et al. UCL/IMF
outcome_underemployed_%: ~10% wage reduction on re-employment — 80%+ due to lower-paying employer
notes: RE-EMPLOYMENT WAGE EFFECTS. Hartz IV reduced re-employment wages by ~10% (diff-in-diff estimate). Workers accepting jobs after exhausting ALG I earn 4-8% lower wages than absent reform. Over 80% of this wage decline is because workers found re-employment at lower-paying employers — occupational or wage downgrade = underemployment. Earnings of displaced workers tracked continuously employed workers closely until 2003 then diverged sharply in 2005 and remained lower through 2010. Low-skilled workers suffered most.
comparability_notes: Wage scarring of -10% is the cleanest cross-comparable metric with Redcar (-0.5% area wages) and China shock wage penalty data. Note that Hartz effect is partially mechanical — reform pressure forces workers to accept lower-paid work. Underemployment rate in traditional sense (% in below-skill jobs) is not directly measured.

source_citation: Price 2020 IZA DP13300
population_n: all workers affected by benefit duration cut
outcome_share_similar_%: PROXY — faster re-employment but lower job quality
notes: RE-EMPLOYMENT SPEED. Hartz IV increased hazard rate of re-employment — probability of experiencing a 1-year jobless spell reduced by 12.4%. Job-finding rate rose steadily in months before benefit exhaustion and spiked sharply at exhaustion point — workers strategically accepting jobs just before benefits run out. Faster re-employment but lower-quality jobs — workers moved into share_similar or underemployed buckets faster under reform pressure.
comparability_notes: Job-finding spike at benefit exhaustion is strategic behaviour not genuine matching. Key model insight: high subsidy_level slows re-employment; low subsidy_level speeds it but increases underemployment share. This is the core policy lever finding from Hartz.

source_citation: Centre for Public Impact + IAB data
outcome_underemployed_%: high — mini-jobs 7.4m by 2010 / temp workers doubled to 780k
notes: LABOUR MARKET SEGMENTATION / UNDEREMPLOYMENT. Mini-jobs (<=€400/month) held by 7.4 million people by Dec 2010. Temporary contract workers doubled to 780000. Ein-Euro-Jobs workfare scheme: 200000+ in 2005 rising to 320000+ in 2009 then declining to 188000 in 2011. Mini-job growth is the clearest measurable underemployment signal — jobs below standard employment threshold. Reforms increased temporary and marginal employment and raised number of people in insecure jobs and at risk of poverty.
comparability_notes: Mini-job count 7.4m is a stock measure of the post-reform labour market not a flow measure of what displaced workers did. Cannot use as a displacement outcome rate directly. However it indicates a common destination for workers exiting unemployment: low-paid insecure work = underemployed bucket.

source_citation: Petrunyk 2023 Wiley + Hochmuth et al. 2020
subsidy_level: ALG II reduced duration for 50+ (15 months max vs 36 months pre-reform)
outcome_exit_%: EXIT — pension system shift in East Germany
notes: OLDER WORKER EXIT. Benefit duration for 50+ cut from up to 36 months to max 15 months (55+ to 18 months). In East Germany: employment remained constant while unemployment fell — decline in unemployment attributed to workers shifting into pension system = EXIT rather than re-employment. Life satisfaction decreased post-reform more for male unemployed in West Germany driven by income decline. Effect stronger on long-term and involuntarily unemployed. Pattern consistent with older workers pushed out of labour force rather than re-employed.
comparability_notes: Directly relevant for Redcar comparison (50%+ of Redcar workers aged 45+). In both cases older workers are the hard-to-place group most likely to exit. Mechanism differs: UK = early retirement via steel pension; Germany = benefit exhaustion then pension system. Exit via pension route inflates apparent re-employment statistics in both episodes.

source_citation: Jacobi and Kluve 2007 — IZA Discussion Paper 2100
notes: RETRAINING (ALMP) EFFECTS. Pre-Hartz ALMP showed negative mean employment effects — training programmes in early 2000s did NOT improve outcomes on average. Post-Hartz reorganisation of public employment services was mainly successful. Voucher-based training (Bildungsgutschein) improved targeting — workers choose course rather than being assigned. Umschulung (full requalification 1-2 years) shows positive long-run effects but lock-in effect during training depresses short-run employment rates. Caseworker assignment still outperforms pure voucher in some studies.
comparability_notes: ALMP = the German equivalent of retraining subsidies in the model. Negative short-run then positive long-run retraining effects is standard finding — model should account for time horizon. Umschulung (1-2 year full requalification) is not comparable to UK training courses (can be 2-day refreshers). Define retrain carefully before comparing.

source_citation: Schneider and Uhlendorff 2006 — IAB/ZAF — Die Wirkung der Hartz-Reform im Bereich der beruflichen Weiterbildung
age_band: all ages 17-65 (58+ were only 0.35% pre-reform / 1.8% post-reform)
subsidy_level: Bildungsgutschein voucher system (Hartz I/II reform of training)
population_n: ~5600 FbW participants matched against ~2.1 million non-participants; FbW stock: ~300k/yr pre-reform / ~100k/yr post-reform
time_horizon: programme duration + up to 18 months follow-up
outcome_retrain_%: NEGATIVE short-run (lock-in) then +5pp employment probability post-programme — see notes
notes: IAB RETRAINING PAPER — CORE FINDINGS. FbW (Foerderung beruflicher Weiterbildung) participant numbers dropped drastically after reform: ~300000/yr pre-reform to ~100000/yr post-reform (67% cut in participation). Average programme duration cut from ~8 months to ~5 months. Main programme type (berufsbezogene und -uebergreifende Weiterbildung = job-related further training without a formal qualification) covered ~60% of pre-reform and ~70% of post-reform entries. During programme: lock-in effect reduces transition rate into employment by ~64% pre-reform and ~83% post-reform — participants less likely to find work than non-participants while in training. After programme: employment probability increases by ~5 percentage points for participants vs matched non-participants. Pre-reform this positive effect only appears after ~22 months. Post-reform: hazard rate out of unemployment after programme end is +88% vs non-participants pre-reform and +111% post-reform (difference not statistically significant). Key reform finding: shorter programmes did NOT harm the positive programme effect — efficiency improved. The +5pp employment effect comes primarily from reduced withdrawal into non-employment (inactivity) rather than from reducing unemployment per se.
comparability_notes: CRITICAL for model calibration: this is the most precise RETRAIN outcome data available. The +5pp employment probability gain is the causal effect of retraining participation. Negative short-run effect (lock-in during programme: ~8 months pre / ~5 months post) must be modelled as a temporary outcome before the positive effect kicks in. Cannot compare FbW participation rate to UK training course counts — these are full structured programmes of months duration. Population is all German unemployed not a displaced cohort — selection into FbW was restricted to those with high re-employment probability so this is a best-case retraining effect.

source_citation: Klinger / Rothe / Weber 2013 — IAB Kurzbericht 11/2013 — Makrooekonomische Perspektive auf die Hartz-Reformen
outcome_exit_%: 40% reduction in unemployment (>5m to 2.90m) / long-term unemployment -46%
notes: IAB MACROECONOMIC EVALUATION — CORE FINDINGS. Unemployment fell 40% from peak of >5 million (2005) to 2.90 million by 2012 — back to early 1990s levels. Long-term unemployment fell 46% over same period. Matching efficiency improved: +10% after Hartz I+II (significant at 99%); +5% after Hartz III (significant at 99%); Hartz IV showed no additional measurable matching improvement. Beveridge curve shifted inward for first time in decades — permanent structural improvement confirmed. At 300000 vacancies: 4.71m unemployed (Feb 2006) fell to 3.40m (Dec 2009). Effect is structural/permanent not just cyclical — confirmed by decomposition of permanent vs cyclical components. Job finding rate rose significantly 2005-2010. Long-term unemployed benefited MORE from matching improvements than short-term unemployed. NEGATIVE SIDE EFFECTS: Real wage index fell 4% between 2003 and 2007 (Statistisches Bundesamt — gross monthly earnings). New jobs for previously unemployed were often unstable — revolving door effect back to ALG II (Grundsicherung). Atypical employment (temp/fixed-term/mini-jobs) increased significantly. Income inequality increased — disproportionate wage declines for lower wage groups. Hard-core long-term unemployed did not benefit sufficiently from reform.
comparability_notes: Matching efficiency +10/+5% is a structural market-level effect — not a worker-level outcome rate. Real wage decline of 4% (2003-2007 gross monthly earnings) is a different measure from the re-employment wage penalty of 4-10% cited in other papers — the IAB figure covers ALL workers including those who kept their jobs and reflects moderate wage settlements. For displaced worker comparison use the 4-10% re-employment wage penalty from Price/Kuegler. Revolving door effect is the most important finding for model calibration: underemployment/exit is not permanent — workers cycle between employment and ALG II. Hard-core long-term unemployed = the exit bucket — reform did not solve their problem.
